title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
source: Original passage written for this demonstration (no ReadWorks content)
content:
Mara Bennett was eleven years old when her family moved to Gull Point, a rocky little island off the coast of Maine. Her father had taken a job as the keeper of the old lighthouse, and he promised that living beside the sea would be the greatest adventure of their lives. Mara was not so sure. She missed her school, her friends, and the noisy streets of Boston. Here, the only sounds were the crashing waves and the cry of the seagulls.

"You will grow to love it," her mother said on the first evening, as they unpacked boxes in the cold kitchen. "Give it a month."

"A month is a very long time," Mara answered quietly.

The lighthouse stood at the highest point of the island. It was a tall white tower with a red roof, and it had been guiding ships safely past the dangerous rocks since 1884. Every night, a powerful lamp turned slowly at the top, sending a beam of light across the dark water. Her father climbed the 112 steps each evening to check the lamp, and each morning he climbed them again to polish the glass.

On the third day, Mara decided to explore. She put on her yellow raincoat and walked along the narrow path that wound down to the beach. The tide was low, and the sand was covered with shells, smooth stones, and long ribbons of green seaweed. She knelt beside a tide pool and found a tiny crab, a purple starfish, and a snail no bigger than a button. For the first time since the move, she smiled.

"Hello, little friends," she whispered. "I suppose we are neighbors now."

As she followed the shoreline, something shiny caught her eye. Half buried in the sand was a small glass bottle, sealed with a cork. Inside was a rolled piece of paper, yellow with age. Mara's heart began to race. She had read about messages in bottles in stories, but she never imagined that she would find one herself.

She carried the bottle carefully back to the lighthouse and showed it to her father. He turned it over in his hands, whistling softly.

"Well, I'll be," he said. "That bottle looks very old. Open it, Mara. It belongs to you."

With trembling fingers, she pulled out the cork and unrolled the paper. The handwriting was faded, but she could still read it. "To whoever finds this," it began. "My name is Thomas Albright, and I am nine years old. Today is June 14, 1962. My grandfather is the keeper of this lighthouse, and I am sending this bottle out to sea to find a new friend. If you read this letter, please write back to me."

At the bottom was an address in a town called Rockport, only forty miles away.

"Sixty years," Mara said in amazement. "This bottle has been floating for sixty years?"

"Or sitting in the sand," her father replied. "The ocean keeps many secrets, and sometimes it gives them back."

The next morning, she sat at the kitchen table with a pencil and a sheet of blue paper. "Dear Thomas," she wrote. "My name is Mara, and I found your bottle. I know it has been a very long time, but I hope this letter finds you well." She told him about the island, the tide pools, and the tall white tower. She told him that she was nervous about starting at a new school in the fall. Then she folded the letter, wrote the old address on the envelope, and her mother helped her find a stamp.

Then, on a bright Saturday morning, a small boat pulled up to the dock. A tall elderly man stepped carefully onto the wooden planks, leaning on a cane. He had white hair, kind eyes, and a letter in his hand.

"I am looking for Mara Bennett," he said with a warm smile.

Mara hurried down the path, her heart pounding. "That's me," she said. "Are you Thomas?"

"I am," the old man replied, and his voice trembled a little. "I received your letter on Wednesday. I have waited sixty years for someone to answer that bottle. I could hardly believe it when I opened the envelope."

Mara's father invited him inside, and her mother made a pot of tea. Thomas sat at the kitchen table and looked around slowly, as if remembering every corner of the room. "My grandfather kept this lighthouse for thirty-one years," he explained. "I spent every summer here when I was a boy. It was the happiest time of my life."

"Would you like to climb to the top?" her father asked at last.

Thomas laughed. "I would love to, but I am afraid that these old knees will not manage 112 steps."

"Then we will go slowly," Mara said, taking his arm. "I will count them for you."

Together, they climbed the spiral staircase, one step at a time, stopping to rest at every landing. When they reached the top, the whole world opened before them: the glittering ocean, the green islands, and the distant white sails. Thomas stood quietly at the window for a long time.

"Thank you, Mara," he finally said. "You gave an old man his childhood back."

From that day on, Thomas visited Gull Point every summer. He taught Mara how to read the tides, how to tie sailor's knots, and how to tell when a storm was coming by watching the clouds. And whenever she felt lonely or afraid, she remembered the bottle in the sand and the lesson it had taught her: that even the smallest message can cross an ocean, and that a new friend may be waiting just beyond the next wave.
